newsitem.title: HONG KONG: CHINA GRAINS - China buys 50,000 tonnes of soybeans.
newsitem.headline: CHINA GRAINS - China buys 50,000 tonnes of soybeans.

text.p: soybeans was sold to China last week for November delivery to the northern province of Shandong, but enquiries are beginning to thin, grain traders said on Thursday.
Some traders said the flood of calls had eased markedly over the past week as November delivery shipments were now more difficult to organise.
"Prompt cargoes are even harder to come by and Chinese buyers may have to settle for December delivery," a Hong Kong-based grains trader said.
Offers for soybeans hovered under $300 per tonne, C and F China on Thursday, while Brazilian meal was offered at $298 per tonne, C and F China for a 20,000-tonne lot on Wednesday.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) soybean futures ended nine to 13 cents per bushel higher on Wednesday with November up 9-1/2 at $6.98-1/2 on rumours that China had bought 50,000 tonnes of beans and was looking for more.

Since the beginning of this month, China has bought about half a million tonnes of soybeans on the CBOT price slide, but sources said buyers had defaulted on about 150,000-200,000 tonnes, grain sources said.
"A number of traders are now in China trying to salvage their deals with customers," said one senior feeds trader.
"It all depends on whether they are willing to lower their prices," he said.
Some Chinese buyers were still anxious about delivery of cargoes prior to January 1, 1997 when China may impose import limits on soybeans, another grain source added.
China may impose quota restrictions on soybean imports starting in 1997 to protect its domestic market, grain and oilseed traders said, but they said there was no official confirmation.

China may also limit importing authority to only two central agencies, fearing that favourable world soybean prices would spark an import flood in 1997, driving down local prices and reducing farmers' incentives to plant soybeans, grains traders said.
But others dismissed the idea as illogical, noting that China's soybean production was dwindling and that the nation's crushing capacity far exceeded its oilseed production.
"China's soybean production this year is less than we thought at 13 million tonnes," said one trader who recently completed a tour of China's northeastern grain producing areas.

In 1995, China had an estimated 1,553 state-owned crushers and 23,631 plants at the county level, with a total capacity of 65 million tonnes per year, said one Western oilseeds source based in China, citing recent research conducted by his firm.
China's 1995 total oilseed production was estimated at 43 million tonnes in the report.
"If you subtract about seven million tonnes of oilseeds for food, you're left with 36 million tonnes of oilseeds and almost double the crushing capacity," the Western source said.
